Neural networks: nn, initializers, stax, optimizers and images

Source: vignettes/neural-networks.Rmd
neural-networks.Rmd
library(jaxR)

JAX is not a neural network framework, but it ships the pieces that such frameworks are built from. jaxR ports all of them:

JAX module jaxR prefix Contents
jax.nn nn_ activations, normalization, attention, one hot encoding
jax.nn.initializers nn_initializers_ weight initializers
jax.example_libraries.stax stax_ a small layer combinator library
jax.example_libraries.optimizers optimizers_ first order optimizers and schedules
jax.image image_ resizing and affine resampling

Activation functions 

x <- jnp_linspace(-3, 3, 7L)
nn_relu(x)
#> Array f32[7]
#> [1] 0 0 0 0 1 2 3
nn_leaky_relu(x, negative_slope = 0.1)
#> Array f32[7]
#> [1] -0.30000001 -0.20000000 -0.09999999  0.00000000  1.00000000  2.00000000
#> [7]  3.00000000
nn_gelu(x)
#> Array f32[7]
#> [1] -0.003637344 -0.045402348 -0.158808008  0.000000000  0.841192007
#> [6]  1.954597712  2.996362686
nn_sigmoid(x)
#> Array f32[7]
#> [1] 0.04742587 0.11920292 0.26894143 0.50000000 0.73105860 0.88079703 0.95257413
nn_softplus(x)
#> Array f32[7]
#> [1] 0.04858735 0.12692800 0.31326172 0.69314718 1.31326175 2.12692809 3.04858732
nn_silu(x)
#> Array f32[7]
#> [1] -0.1422776 -0.2384058 -0.2689414  0.0000000  0.7310586  1.7615941  2.8577223

The full set: nn_relu, nn_relu6, nn_leaky_relu, nn_elu, nn_celu, nn_selu, nn_gelu, nn_glu, nn_silu (alias nn_swish), nn_mish, nn_sigmoid, nn_log_sigmoid, nn_hard_sigmoid, nn_hard_silu (alias nn_hard_swish), nn_tanh, nn_hard_tanh, nn_soft_sign, nn_softplus, nn_sparse_plus, nn_sparse_sigmoid, nn_squareplus, nn_identity, nn_log1mexp.

As in JAX, nn_relu has a custom derivative so that its gradient at zero is zero:

grad(nn_relu)(0)
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 0
vmap(grad(nn_gelu))(x)
#> Array f32[7]
#> [1] -0.01158401 -0.08609934 -0.08296407  0.50000000  1.08296394  1.08609939
#> [7]  1.01158392

Normalization along an axis 

logits <- as_jax(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 1), 2, byrow = TRUE))
nn_softmax(logits)                 # last axis by default
#> Array f32[2,3]
#>            [,1]      [,2]      [,3]
#> [1,] 0.09003057 0.2447285 0.6652409
#> [2,] 0.33333334 0.3333333 0.3333333
nn_log_softmax(logits, axis = 0L)
#> Array f32[2,3]
#>            [,1]       [,2]      [,3]
#> [1,] -0.6931472 -0.3132616 -0.126928
#> [2,] -0.6931472 -1.3132616 -2.126928
nn_logsumexp(logits, axis = 1L)
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] 3.407606 2.098612
nn_logmeanexp(logits, axis = 1L)
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] 2.308994 1.000000
nn_standardize(logits, axis = 1L)
#> Array f32[2,3]
#>           [,1] [,2]     [,3]
#> [1,] -1.224735    0 1.224735
#> [2,]  0.000000    0 0.000000

The where argument restricts a reduction to selected elements:

mask <- as_jax(matrix(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE), 2, byrow = TRUE))
nn_softmax(logits, where = mask)
#> Array f32[2,3]
#>           [,1]      [,2]      [,3]
#> [1,] 0.2689414 0.7310586 0.0000000
#> [2,] 0.3333333 0.3333333 0.3333333

One hot encoding

Class labels are 0-based.

nn_one_hot(c(0L, 2L, 1L), 3L)
#> Array f32[3,3]
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    0    0
#> [2,]    0    0    1
#> [3,]    0    1    0

Attention

nn_dot_product_attention(query, key, value) takes arrays of shape (batch, length, heads, head_dim) (the batch axis is optional) and supports masks, bias, causal attention and sequence lengths.

k <- random_split(random_key(0L), 3L)
q <- random_normal(k[0], c(4L, 2L, 8L))    # T = 4, heads = 2, dim = 8
kk <- random_normal(k[1], c(5L, 2L, 8L))   # S = 5
v <- random_normal(k[2], c(5L, 2L, 8L))
dim(nn_dot_product_attention(q, kk, v))
#> [1] 4 2 8
dim(nn_dot_product_attention(q, q, q, is_causal = TRUE))
#> [1] 4 2 8

Initializers

An initializer is a function of a key and a shape. The constructors mirror jax.nn.initializers.

init <- nn_initializers_glorot_normal()
W <- init(random_key(0L), c(256L, 128L))
dim(W)
#> [1] 256 128
jnp_std(W)                 # close to sqrt(2 / (256 + 128)) = 0.072
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 0.07230617

nn_initializers_he_uniform()(random_key(1L), c(2L, 3L))
#> Array f32[2,3]
#>            [,1]      [,2]       [,3]
#> [1,] -0.2125833 0.1169235 -0.1873444
#> [2,] -0.2134013 1.3765051  0.2041950
nn_initializers_orthogonal()(random_key(2L), c(3L, 3L))
#> Array f32[3,3]
#>           [,1]          [,2]       [,3]
#> [1,] 0.2603413  0.8658641577  0.4272021
#> [2,] 0.8542019 -0.0003046883 -0.5199414
#> [3,] 0.4500686 -0.5002790093  0.7397021
nn_initializers_constant(0.5)(random_key(3L), 3L)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 0.5 0.5 0.5

Available: zeros, ones, constant, uniform, normal, truncated_normal, variance_scaling, glorot_uniform (alias xavier_uniform), glorot_normal (alias xavier_normal), lecun_uniform, lecun_normal, he_uniform (alias kaiming_uniform), he_normal (alias kaiming_normal), orthogonal and delta_orthogonal.

stax: layers as pairs of functions

A stax layer is a pair list(init_fun, apply_fun). init_fun(rng, input_shape) returns the output shape and the parameters; apply_fun(params, inputs, ...) computes the output. Combinators build networks out of layers. A batch dimension of unknown size is written -1L.

net <- stax_serial(
  stax_Dense(32L), stax_Relu,
  stax_Dense(32L), stax_Relu,
  stax_Dense(1L))

res <- net$init_fun(random_key(0L), c(-1L, 2L))
res[[1]]                                   # output shape
#> [1] -1  1
params <- res[[2]]
length(tree_leaves(params))                # three weight matrices, three biases
#> [1] 6

X <- random_normal(random_key(1L), c(5L, 2L))
net$apply_fun(params, X)
#> Array f32[5,1]
#>              [,1]
#> [1,]  0.024520740
#> [2,] -0.007830322
#> [3,]  0.004498099
#> [4,] -0.020521889
#> [5,]  0.097488366

Layers: stax_Dense, stax_Conv, stax_GeneralConv, stax_ConvTranspose, stax_Conv1DTranspose, stax_GeneralConvTranspose, stax_BatchNorm, stax_Dropout, stax_MaxPool, stax_AvgPool, stax_SumPool, stax_Flatten, stax_Identity, the activations stax_Relu, stax_LeakyRelu, stax_Elu, stax_Selu, stax_Gelu, stax_Sigmoid, stax_Tanh, stax_Softplus, stax_Softmax, stax_LogSoftmax, stax_Exp, and the combinators stax_serial, stax_parallel, stax_FanOut, stax_FanInSum, stax_FanInConcat, stax_elementwise and stax_shape_dependent.

A convolutional network on images in NHWC layout:

cnn <- stax_serial(
  stax_Conv(8L, c(3L, 3L), padding = "SAME"), stax_Relu,
  stax_MaxPool(c(2L, 2L), strides = c(2L, 2L)),
  stax_Flatten,
  stax_Dense(10L), stax_LogSoftmax)
out <- cnn$init_fun(random_key(0L), c(-1L, 8L, 8L, 1L))
out[[1]]
#> [1]  0 10
imgs <- random_normal(random_key(5L), c(2L, 8L, 8L, 1L))
dim(cnn$apply_fun(out[[2]], imgs))
#> [1]  2 10

A residual block with stax_FanOut and stax_FanInSum:

block <- stax_serial(
  stax_FanOut(2L),
  stax_parallel(stax_serial(stax_Dense(4L), stax_Tanh), stax_Identity),
  stax_FanInSum)
p <- block$init_fun(random_key(0L), c(-1L, 4L))[[2]]
dim(block$apply_fun(p, jnp_ones(c(3L, 4L))))
#> [1] 3 4

Layers with randomness (stax_Dropout) take the key through the rng argument of apply_fun.

Optimizers

An optimizer is a triple init_fn, update_fn, params_fn. The state is a pytree, so an update step can be compiled with jit.

# Data from a noisy sine
key <- random_key(7L)
X <- random_uniform(key, c(128L, 1L), minval = -3, maxval = 3)
y <- jnp_sin(X) + 0.1 * random_normal(random_fold_in(key, 1L), c(128L, 1L))

net <- stax_serial(stax_Dense(32L), stax_Tanh, stax_Dense(32L), stax_Tanh, stax_Dense(1L))
params <- net$init_fun(random_key(0L), c(-1L, 1L))[[2]]
loss <- function(params, X, y) jnp_mean((net$apply_fun(params, X) - y)^2)

opt <- optimizers_adam(step_size = 0.01)
state <- opt$init_fn(params)

step <- jit(function(i, state, X, y) {
  g <- grad(loss)(opt$params_fn(state), X, y)
  opt$update_fn(i, g, state)
})

loss(params, X, y)
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 1.115495
for (i in 0:299) state <- step(i, state, X, y)
loss(opt$params_fn(state), X, y)
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 0.008867357

Optimizers: optimizers_sgd, optimizers_momentum, optimizers_nesterov, optimizers_adagrad, optimizers_rmsprop, optimizers_rmsprop_momentum, optimizers_adam, optimizers_adamax and optimizers_sm3. The step size is a number or a schedule (a function of the step):

sched <- optimizers_exponential_decay(0.1, decay_steps = 100, decay_rate = 0.5)
sched(0)
#> [1] 0.1
sched(200)
#> [1] 0.025
pw <- optimizers_piecewise_constant(c(100L, 200L), c(0.1, 0.01, 0.001))
pw(150)
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 0.01
opt2 <- optimizers_momentum(sched, mass = 0.9)

Schedules: optimizers_constant, optimizers_exponential_decay, optimizers_inverse_time_decay, optimizers_polynomial_decay, optimizers_piecewise_constant and optimizers_make_schedule. Gradient utilities:

g <- grad(loss)(params, X, y)
optimizers_l2_norm(g)
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 5.546106
optimizers_l2_norm(optimizers_clip_grads(g, 0.1))
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 0.09999999

optimizers_optimizer() turns an optimizer written for a single array into one that works on any pytree, exactly like the @optimizer decorator, and optimizers_unpack_optimizer_state() / optimizers_pack_optimizer_state() convert the state to and from a plain pytree for saving.

Images

image_resize and image_scale_and_translate port jax.image. Methods: "nearest", "linear" (alias "bilinear", "trilinear", "triangle"), "cubic" (alias "bicubic", "tricubic"), "cubic-pytorch", "lanczos3" and "lanczos5"; they are also listed in image_ResizeMethod.

img <- jnp_reshape(jnp_arange(16, dtype = "float32"), c(4L, 4L))
image_resize(img, c(2L, 2L), method = "linear")
#> Array f32[2,2]
#>          [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 3.571429  5.142858
#> [2,] 9.857144 11.428574
dim(image_resize(img, c(8L, 8L), method = "cubic"))
#> [1] 8 8
image_resize(img, c(4L, 2L), method = "nearest")
#> Array f32[4,2]
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1    3
#> [2,]    5    7
#> [3,]    9   11
#> [4,]   13   15

# Scale by 2 and shift by one pixel along both spatial axes
image_scale_and_translate(img, c(4L, 4L), spatial_dims = c(0L, 1L),
                          scale = c(2, 2), translation = c(1, 1), method = "linear")
#> Array f32[4,4]
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    0    0 0.00 0.00
#> [2,]    0    0 0.25 0.75
#> [3,]    0    1 1.25 1.75
#> [4,]    0    3 3.25 3.75

Both functions are differentiable with respect to the image, and image_scale_and_translate also with respect to scale and translation:

grad(function(s) jnp_sum(image_scale_and_translate(
  img, c(4L, 4L), c(0L, 1L), s, as_jax(c(0, 0)), "linear")^2))(as_jax(c(1.5, 1.5)))
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] -666.9630 -129.1852
